title: Harness Patterns
description: Software design patterns mapped onto AI agent harness engineering, in plain English.

chapters.title: The Agent Loop
chapters.summary: An AI agent works in a loop. It reads what has happened so far, asks the model what to do next, does it, and repeats until the job is done. The patterns in this chapter shape that loop: what stage it is in, where extra checks can plug in, how the model's reply is turned into actions, and how a run can be paused, resumed or rolled back.

chapters.title: The Tool System
chapters.summary: A model can only write text. Tools are what let it act: read a file, search the web, send an email. This chapter shows how a tool request is packaged, found, created, wrapped with checks and finally run. Most of the classic object-oriented patterns find a home here.

chapters.title: The Model Call Layer
chapters.kick: Chapter 3 · Talking to the AI model
chapters.summary: The model lives on someone else's servers. It can be busy, slow, or briefly down, it limits how much you can send, it charges for every word, and its replies are not always perfectly formatted. These patterns keep requests flowing anyway: picking a provider, trying again, switching to a backup, saving repeat work, and counting the cost.

chapters.title: Context and Memory
chapters.summary: The model can only see a limited amount of text at once (its context window), and that space is costly. Conversations, files and saved memories are large and need to last. These patterns decide what gets stored, when it is loaded, how copies are avoided, and how two people editing at once do not overwrite each other.

chapters.title: Multi-Agent Orchestration
chapters.summary: One agent eventually runs out of room or time. Several agents can split the work and run side by side, but then they must coordinate, pass messages and be tracked. These patterns come from large distributed systems, where those problems were solved first.

chapters.title: Async, Concurrency and Scheduling
chapters.kick: Chapter 6 · Work that has to wait
chapters.summary: Agents spend a lot of time waiting: for the model, for tools, for a person to approve, or for a scheduled time. These patterns let the system run many jobs at once, hand work to background workers, pause for approval, and shut down cleanly without two jobs tripping over each other.

chapters.title: Safety, Permissions and Resilience
chapters.kick: Chapter 7 · Keeping agents within safe limits
chapters.summary: An agent acts on someone's behalf using real logins and real data. These patterns put checks between what the agent wants to do and what actually happens: filters, permission rules, walls between customers, actions that never run twice by accident, and cleanup that always happens.

chapters.title: Harness Architecture
chapters.summary: Zoom out and the whole system has a shape: a core that knows how agents work, with clear connection points for models, tools, storage and the screens people use. These patterns decide that shape and how it can grow without becoming a tangle.

chapters.title: Functional Plumbing
chapters.summary: A lot of agent work is data passing through steps: messages become a prompt, the model's reply becomes tool requests, tool results become a summary. Functional patterns keep each step small and easy to chain together safely.

chapters.title: The Harness Frontend
chapters.kick: Chapter 10 · Where people meet the agent
chapters.summary: A chat window looks simple, but behind it the reply arrives word by word, tool activity appears as cards, approval buttons pop up, and documents open beside the chat. These patterns organise the screen side of the system.

chapters.title: Performance Internals
chapters.summary: Two patterns from video game engines help when an agent platform serves many users: keep data that is used together stored together, and divide data into areas so a search only looks where the answer can be.

chapters.title: Testing and Evals
chapters.summary: AI agents do not give the same answer every time, so tests need extra structure. These patterns organise test cases, sample data, fake services and automated browser checks.

chapters.title: Code-Level Idioms
chapters.summary: The last few patterns are small habits inside the code. They do not shape the whole system, but they keep everyday code tidy and they show up in almost every project.

chapters.title: How this book was checked
chapters.summary: After the book was written, every entry was checked again by a separate reviewer acting as a senior architect for business AI platforms. Each entry was compared with three things: the pattern's original definition in the standard books, how real agent systems actually behave, and what large companies need (keeping customers' data apart, controlling who can do what, keeping records for audits, protecting personal data, controlling cost, and seeing what the system is doing). Mistakes were fixed in place, and every entry gained an "In a large company" note. This appendix lists what was found and what changed.

chapters.title: Glossary
chapters.summary: Short, plain explanations of the technical words used in this book. Each entry also explains these words where they first appear, so you only need this page as a reminder.

patterns.title: Game Loop
patterns.gist: Run the agent as a loop: build the request, call the model, run any tools it asks for, and repeat until it stops asking.
patterns.figure_caption: The run is one cycle, repeated until the model stops asking for tools.

patterns.title: Update Method
patterns.gist: Give each part of the harness its own update hook, and let the loop call every hook once per turn.
patterns.figure_caption: The loop knows one call, and each subsystem decides what that call does.

patterns.title: State
patterns.gist: Make each phase of the loop its own state object, so each state decides how to react to messages, interrupts and tool results.
patterns.figure_caption: Each state owns its own transitions, so a tool cannot run before approval.

patterns.title: Template Method
patterns.gist: Fix the order of a turn's steps in a base class, and let each agent type change only the hooks it needs.
patterns.figure_caption: The outline is fixed, and subclasses fill in only the marked slots.

patterns.title: Chain of Responsibility
patterns.gist: Pass each tool call through an ordered chain of hooks that can block, change or pass it on. Only the chain's end lets it run.
patterns.figure_caption: Each hook can stop the call or pass it to the next one.

patterns.title: Interpreter
patterns.gist: Read the model's structured output as action objects from a small grammar (a set of language rules), then run them on the workspace.
patterns.figure_caption: Text becomes a tree of nodes, and each node knows how to run itself.

patterns.title: Memento
patterns.gist: Save a snapshot of the session's messages and file edits before each risky step, so the user can go back to any earlier turn.
patterns.figure_caption: The session makes and reads snapshots, and the store only keeps them.

patterns.title: Iterator
patterns.gist: Go through stream events, turns or stored messages one at a time with next(), without loading or exposing the whole source.
patterns.figure_caption: Consumers pull one item at a time and never see the source behind it.

patterns.title: Composite
patterns.gist: Treat a message, a tool result and a single text block through the same interface, because content blocks sit inside each other.
patterns.figure_caption: Containers and leaves answer the same call, so the caller never checks types.

patterns.title: Visitor
patterns.gist: Keep content block classes stable, and put each operation that runs across them, like token counting or redaction, in its own visitor class.
patterns.figure_caption: Blocks send the call to the right method, and operations live in visitors.

patterns.title: Acyclic Visitor
patterns.gist: Let each visitor handle only the block types it knows, so a new content block type never forces edits elsewhere.
patterns.figure_caption: The block asks the visitor what it handles, so visitors never list every type.

patterns.title: Double Dispatch
patterns.gist: Choose the handler from two runtime types at once: the incoming event's type and the session's current state.
patterns.figure_caption: The event type picks the method, and the current state picks its behaviour.

patterns.title: Callback
patterns.gist: Pass functions into the loop, and the loop calls them when a token streams in, a tool finishes or a turn ends.
patterns.figure_caption: The client hands over functions, and the loop calls them at the right moments.

patterns.title: Context Object
patterns.gist: Bundle everything one turn needs (ids, budget, working folder, permissions, cancel signal) into one object passed to every component.
patterns.figure_caption: One object carries the turn's facts to every component that needs them.

patterns.title: Collecting Parameter
patterns.gist: Pass one collector object through a series of steps, so each step adds its findings instead of returning separate results to merge.
patterns.figure_caption: One list travels through every check and fills up along the way.

patterns.title: Pipeline
patterns.gist: Prepare context in fixed stages: find candidates, rerank them by relevance, shorten the best ones, then insert them into the prompt.
patterns.figure_caption: Each stage narrows the data and passes it on.

patterns.title: Rule Engine
patterns.gist: Check a set of written rules against each turn's facts to decide routing, approvals and compaction, without hard-coded branches.
patterns.figure_caption: Facts go in, rules match, and the matching actions come out.

patterns.title: Trampoline
patterns.gist: Run deep recursive planning as a flat loop, where each step returns the next step instead of calling it.
patterns.figure_caption: The driver keeps the call stack flat by running each returned step itself.

patterns.title: Command
patterns.gist: Turn every tool call into an object that the harness can queue, log, approve, retry or undo.
patterns.figure_caption: A tool call becomes a command object before anything runs it.

patterns.title: Strategy
patterns.gist: Keep one tool name and schema, but swap the code behind it, such as which backend a search tool uses.
patterns.figure_caption: The tool's name and schema stay fixed while the backend behind it is swapped.

patterns.title: Adapter
patterns.gist: Wrap MCP servers and outside APIs so each one looks like a native tool, with the harness's own name, schema and run method.
patterns.figure_caption: Each foreign interface gets one adapter, so the loop only ever calls Tool.run().

patterns.title: Converter
patterns.gist: Translate tool specs, calls and results between the harness's own types and each provider's wire format, in both directions.
patterns.figure_caption: One converter owns every mapping between internal types and the wire, both ways.

patterns.title: Facade
patterns.gist: Give the model one simple tool that hides a many-step system, so the model makes one call instead of five.
patterns.figure_caption: The model makes one call, and the facade drives four parts and returns a short summary.

patterns.title: Registry
patterns.gist: Keep one map from names to tools, which the harness uses to list tools for the model and to route each tool_use call.
patterns.figure_caption: Every tool enters through one map, which both lists the tools and finds each call.

patterns.title: Factory
patterns.gist: Create tools from a name and a config entry, so agent definitions list tools as data instead of building them in code.
patterns.figure_caption: Names in config go in, and finished tools with shared dependencies come out.

patterns.title: Factory Method
patterns.gist: Let a base runner own the agent workflow, while each subclass decides which executor or tool it creates.
patterns.figure_caption: The base class owns the loop, and each subclass only decides which shell is created.

patterns.title: Abstract Factory
patterns.gist: Create a whole matching family of tools, such as a shell and a file system, for one environment, so local and sandboxed tools never mix.
patterns.figure_caption: Choosing one factory chooses the whole family, so environments never mix.

patterns.title: Factory Kit
patterns.gist: Build a frozen kit of named tool builders once at startup, then make exactly the tool set each agent profile asks for.
patterns.figure_caption: Builders are registered once and frozen, and each profile picks names and gets fresh tools.

patterns.title: Builder
patterns.gist: Put together a large model request piece by piece, from system blocks, tools, history, cache breakpoints and limits, then check it once.
patterns.figure_caption: Parts arrive from different places, and build() checks them together before sending.

patterns.title: Step Builder
patterns.gist: Force a subagent or request spec through its required steps in a set order, so build() is out of reach until each is set.
patterns.figure_caption: Each step type offers only the next call, so build() is out of reach until all are set.

patterns.title: Prototype
patterns.gist: Copy a tuned agent or tool config template and change only a few fields, instead of building each version from scratch.
patterns.figure_caption: Each subagent starts as a deep copy of one tuned template plus a small change.

patterns.title: Proxy
patterns.gist: Put a permission and sandbox layer with the same interface in front of every real tool, so nothing runs without passing its checks.
patterns.figure_caption: Every call passes the proxy's rules, approval and sandbox before the real tool runs.

patterns.title: Virtual Proxy
patterns.gist: Use a light stub in place of a costly tool, and load its full schema or start its server only when first needed.
patterns.figure_caption: The stub costs one line in the prompt, and the real tool loads once, on first use.

patterns.title: Dynamic Proxy
patterns.gist: Build tool stand-ins while the program runs, from JSON schemas, and send every call through one shared handler.
patterns.figure_caption: Stubs are built from schemas, and every stub sends its call to one handler

patterns.title: Decorator
patterns.gist: Wrap a tool in layers such as logging, retries, rate limits and telemetry. Each layer adds one job behind the same interface.
patterns.figure_caption: Each wrapper adds one job and passes the same call inward

patterns.title: Delegation
patterns.gist: A tool hands the real work to a helper object or a subagent, then returns that answer as its own result.
patterns.figure_caption: The caller sees one call and one answer. The delegate does the work.

patterns.title: Servant
patterns.gist: Put shared chores, like checking paths or shortening results, in one helper that many tools call, not a copy per tool.
patterns.figure_caption: Many tools hand their data to the same two helpers

patterns.title: Null Object
patterns.gist: When a feature is switched off, plug in a helper that does nothing, so the agent loop never checks for None.
patterns.figure_caption: The loop calls the same interface, and a do-nothing version fills the gap

patterns.title: Special Case
patterns.gist: For expected odd outcomes, like no matches or file not found, return a special result object that knows how to behave.
patterns.figure_caption: An empty search returns a real object that can explain itself

patterns.title: Extension Objects
patterns.gist: Let harness parts ask a tool, while running, for optional extras such as streaming, undo or preview, without enlarging every tool's interface.
patterns.figure_caption: The same question gets an extension from one tool and None from another

patterns.title: Marker Interface
patterns.gist: Tag tools as read-only, destructive or approval-required with empty markers. The permission gate checks them before running anything.
patterns.figure_caption: The gate routes calls by their tags, not by what the tools do

patterns.title: Type Object
patterns.gist: Define each tool as a data record (name, schema, handler) instead of a new class, so adding a tool adds no code.
patterns.figure_caption: New tools arrive as records that point at a few shared handlers

patterns.title: Bytecode
patterns.gist: The model writes a short program in a limited action language. A small harness VM checks it, then runs it step by step.
patterns.figure_caption: The model writes data, and only the VM's fixed opcodes ever touch the world

patterns.title: Abstract Document
patterns.gist: Keep a tool call's extra details in one flexible key-value document. Small typed views read only what each part needs.
patterns.figure_caption: One document collects every property, and each reader sees it through its own view

patterns.title: Property
patterns.gist: Give each tool a settings map that falls back to a parent map. Tools inherit defaults and change only what differs.
patterns.figure_caption: A lookup climbs the chain until some level has the key

patterns.title: Parameter Object
patterns.gist: Bundle a tool's many arguments into one typed request object. Check it once and pass it along whole.
patterns.figure_caption: Loose JSON is parsed once into a typed request that travels whole

patterns.title: Execute Around
patterns.gist: Run every tool inside a function that sets up the sandbox first and always cleans it up afterwards, even on failure.
patterns.figure_caption: Setup and cleanup belong to the wrapper, so no tool can skip them

patterns.title: Fluent Interface
patterns.gist: Set up an agent with chained method calls that read like a sentence. Each call returns the builder for the next.
patterns.figure_caption: Every call returns the same builder until build() checks and freezes it

patterns.title: Gateway
patterns.gist: Send every model call through one client that holds the keys, picks a provider and switches over when one is down.
patterns.figure_caption: Callers see one client. Routing, keys and failover live behind it.

patterns.title: Ambassador
patterns.gist: Run a sidecar, a helper beside the harness, that owns the model connection: keys, TLS encryption, retries, timeouts and telemetry.
patterns.figure_caption: The agent speaks plain HTTP locally. The sidecar deals with the outside world.

patterns.title: Bridge
patterns.gist: Keep the family of agent types apart from the family of model backends, so each side can grow without a class for every pair.
patterns.figure_caption: Two families grow on their own, joined by one reference.

patterns.title: Retry
patterns.gist: Re-send a model call that failed for a short-lived reason, waiting longer each time, and give up after a fixed limit.
patterns.figure_caption: Each failure earns a longer, jittered wait before the same request goes again.

patterns.title: Fallback
patterns.gist: When the preferred model cannot answer, give the same request to a substitute, so the turn still finishes, maybe at lower quality.
patterns.figure_caption: The same request walks down a fixed chain until something answers.

patterns.title: Circuit Breaker
patterns.gist: Stop calling a provider that keeps failing, refuse calls quickly for a cool-down period, then let one test call decide whether to resume.
patterns.figure_caption: Three states: pass calls, refuse them fast, or test with one probe.

patterns.title: Rate Limiting
patterns.gist: Cap how many requests and tokens each caller may use per time window, and refuse the extra with a clear time to retry.
patterns.figure_caption: Each tenant spends from its own bucket. Overdrafts are refused with a wait time.

patterns.title: Throttling
patterns.gist: Keep the harness's own agents within a safe share of the provider quota by pacing, capping, degrading or delaying their calls.
patterns.figure_caption: A burst queues on the ramp and leaves at an even pace set by the headers.

patterns.title: Load Shedding
patterns.gist: When demand is more than capacity, drop or delay the least important model work, so interactive turns keep getting answers.
patterns.figure_caption: Under load, low-priority calls are put off so the chat stays fast.

patterns.title: Backpressure
patterns.gist: Let a slow consumer push back on its producer, so work waits at the source instead of piling up in memory.
patterns.figure_caption: A full buffer makes the producer wait instead of piling up work.

patterns.title: Queue-Based Load Leveling
patterns.gist: Put model jobs in a durable queue that a fixed pool of workers empties, so bursts become a steady, affordable call rate.
patterns.figure_caption: Bursts fill the queue. Workers empty it at the rate the model can take.

patterns.title: Caching
patterns.gist: Reuse work already paid for: cache the stable start of the prompt with the provider, and save repeatable tool results locally.
patterns.figure_caption: A hit skips the expensive work. A miss pays once and fills the cache.

patterns.title: Object Pool
patterns.gist: Keep costly resources such as sandboxes, browsers and connections ready, lend them to agents, and reset them when returned.
patterns.figure_caption: Borrow, use, reset, return: nothing expensive is built for each call.

patterns.title: Multiton
patterns.gist: Keep exactly one client per key, such as provider and model or tenant, created on first use and shared after that.
patterns.figure_caption: Same key, same instance. A new key creates exactly one more.

patterns.title: Singleton
patterns.gist: Share one model client and settings object across the whole process, so every agent uses the same connection pool, credentials and limits.
patterns.figure_caption: Every caller reaches the one client, which owns the only connection pool.

patterns.title: Tolerant Reader
patterns.gist: Read model output by taking what you need and ignoring the rest, fixing small mistakes instead of crashing on them.
patterns.figure_caption: Messy text goes in, a strict typed object comes out, and the model is asked again only when it truly matters.

patterns.title: Partial Response
patterns.gist: Deliver a model's answer piece by piece as it is written, or send only the fields a caller asked for.
patterns.figure_caption: Text reaches the user as it arrives. Tools run only once the message is complete.

patterns.title: Money
patterns.gist: Store tokens and cost as typed amounts with a unit or currency, so sums, budgets and reports cannot mix numbers that do not match.
patterns.figure_caption: Counts become typed tokens, then typed money, before anything is added up.

patterns.title: Repository
patterns.gist: Give the agent's memory a simple list-like interface (add, search, remove), so loop code never talks to the database directly.
patterns.figure_caption: The loop asks one collection, and the repository decides which store answers

patterns.title: DAOData Access Object
patterns.gist: Wrap one storage system's raw API in a small object with plain append, load and delete calls for one record type.
patterns.figure_caption: Callers see four simple actions, and SQL, pooling and encoding stay inside the DAO

patterns.title: DAO Factory
patterns.gist: Choose a storage system once at startup and get a matching set of DAOs (transcripts, memories, artifacts) that all use it.
patterns.figure_caption: Choosing the factory chooses every DAO, so stores never mix

patterns.title: Data Mapper
patterns.gist: Keep objects like Memory and Turn unaware of storage by putting a separate mapper between them and the store.
patterns.figure_caption: Neither side knows the other's shape, and only the mapper knows both

patterns.title: DTOData Transfer Object
patterns.gist: Send flat, versioned data objects with no behaviour between separate processes, such as the tool runner and the chat client.
patterns.figure_caption: Only flat, versioned data crosses the process boundary

patterns.title: Value Object
patterns.gist: Treat content blocks, messages and token counts as values that never change and are compared by content, so sharing and caching them is safe.
patterns.figure_caption: Equal content means equal objects, and a change makes a new object

patterns.title: Composite Entity
patterns.gist: Load and save a whole session (messages, todos, tool state, files read) as one unit through a single root object.
patterns.figure_caption: Everything that belongs to a session moves through one root

patterns.title: Unit of Work
patterns.gist: Collect a turn's memory, todo and message writes, then save them all together at the end of the turn, or cancel them all.
patterns.figure_caption: Writes wait in the unit of work until the end of the turn decides what happens to them

patterns.title: Identity Map
patterns.gist: Keep one in-memory object per document id while building context, so a file or memory found twice enters the window once.
patterns.figure_caption: Three retrievals of the same chunk become one object in context

patterns.title: Lazy Loading
patterns.gist: Put short placeholders for tool schemas and file contents into context, and load the full version only when the agent asks.
patterns.figure_caption: Only the schema the model asks for ever enters the context

patterns.title: Flyweight
patterns.gist: Share one unchangeable copy of the system prompt and tool schemas across thousands of sessions, keeping only each session's own state separate.
patterns.figure_caption: Thousands of sessions point at one shared prompt bundle

patterns.title: Write-Ahead Log
patterns.gist: Write each tool call to a lasting log before running it, so a crashed run can restart exactly where it stopped.
patterns.figure_caption: The plan reaches the disk before the tool runs, so a crash leaves a readable trail

patterns.title: Event Sourcing
patterns.gist: Store a session as events that are only ever added, and rebuild any view (model context, chat UI, a fork) by replaying them.
patterns.figure_caption: The log is the truth, and every view is rebuilt from it

patterns.title: Dirty Flag
patterns.gist: Mark a memory or summary as changed when its source changes, and re-embed or re-summarise only when that mark is set.
patterns.figure_caption: Only changed notes pay for a new embedding

patterns.title: Serialized Entity
patterns.gist: Save a whole live object, such as an agent checkpoint, as one blob of data that can be stored, sent and restored elsewhere.
patterns.figure_caption: The whole run folds into one blob and unfolds on another worker

patterns.title: Serialized LOB
patterns.gist: Store a transcript or artifact body as one packed blob column, in a row whose other columns stay small and searchable.
patterns.figure_caption: Small columns are the label, and the transcript travels sealed in one field

patterns.title: Metadata Mapping
patterns.gist: Describe how memory records map to store fields in one table of settings, and let shared code do every load and save.
patterns.figure_caption: One generic engine follows a declared map instead of code for each type

patterns.title: Single Table Inheritance
patterns.gist: Save every kind of transcript event in one table with a kind column, leaving empty the fields a kind does not use.
patterns.figure_caption: Every event kind lands in one table, told apart by its kind column

patterns.title: Table Inheritance
patterns.gist: Keep fields shared by all events in a base table, and each kind's own fields in a separate table linked by event id.
patterns.figure_caption: Shared fields live once, and each kind adds its own table on the same id

patterns.title: Optimistic Offline Lock
patterns.gist: Let the agent and a person edit one document without locks, and check at save time whether someone changed it first.
patterns.figure_caption: No one waits, and the late writer finds out at save time and merges

patterns.title: Version Number
patterns.gist: Stamp every stored artifact, memory and session with a counter that goes up on each write, so stale reads and writes can be caught.
patterns.figure_caption: Both writers read v4, and the counter lets only the first one win

patterns.title: Sharding
patterns.gist: Split session and memory stores by tenant, so each shard holds one slice of the data and each turn touches one shard.
patterns.figure_caption: The tenant's region limits the choice, and the hash only picks a shard inside it

patterns.title: Client Session
patterns.gist: Keep the conversation on the client, which sends the full message history with every request, so the server stores nothing between calls.
patterns.figure_caption: The client carries the whole conversation, so any replica can answer

patterns.title: Server Session
patterns.gist: Keep the conversation, sandbox and files on the server under a session id, and the client sends only the id and new message.
patterns.figure_caption: The client holds a ticket, and the server holds the conversation

patterns.title: Actor Model
patterns.gist: Run each subagent as a sealed-off actor that keeps its own context and only reacts to messages in its mailbox.
patterns.figure_caption: Subagents share nothing. Work and results move only as messages between mailboxes.

patterns.title: Mediator
patterns.gist: Send all subagent coordination through one orchestrator, so specialists never need to know about or message each other.
patterns.figure_caption: Every subagent talks to the orchestrator, and none of them talk to each other.

patterns.title: Master-Worker
patterns.gist: A master agent splits a big job into separate tasks, gives them to worker subagents, and collects or reassigns the results.
patterns.figure_caption: The master owns the task table, so a lost task simply goes back to pending.

patterns.title: Fork/Join
patterns.gist: Split a task into parts for parallel subagents, maybe splitting again, and continue only when every child has finished.
patterns.figure_caption: Each parent forks its children and continues only after joining all of them.

patterns.title: Fan-Out/Fan-In
patterns.gist: Send the same question to several subagents at once, then gather their answers in one place, usually by a deadline.
patterns.figure_caption: One question goes out to many. One bundle comes back when all reply or the clock runs out.

patterns.title: MapReduce
patterns.gist: Turn each document into short notes with its own subagent, group the notes by theme, then combine each group into one summary.
patterns.figure_caption: No call ever sees all the documents. Maps shrink them, the shuffle groups, and reducers combine.

patterns.title: Leader-Followers
patterns.gist: Worker agents take turns. One leader watches the task queue, claims the next task, then makes a follower the new leader.
patterns.figure_caption: Leadership rotates. The leader claims a task, promotes a follower, and rejoins the line when done.

patterns.title: Leader Election
patterns.gist: Let a group of identical agents agree on exactly one coordinator, and pick a new one automatically when it disappears.
patterns.figure_caption: An atomic lease picks one leader. When it expires, the next one takes over with a higher term.

patterns.title: Observer
patterns.gist: Let the UI, the orchestrator and loggers watch a shared task list and react when a subagent changes an item.
patterns.figure_caption: The task list itself calls every attached observer when an item changes.

patterns.title: Publish-Subscribe
patterns.gist: Agents publish events such as file.changed or task.done to named topics, and every agent subscribed to a topic gets them.
patterns.figure_caption: Publishers name a topic, never a receiver. The broker sends each event on to all its subscribers.

patterns.title: Event Aggregator
patterns.gist: Collect events from every harness part in one hub, so listeners sign up once instead of connecting to each source.
patterns.figure_caption: Sources and listeners each know one object, the hub, instead of each other.

patterns.title: Data Bus
patterns.gist: Connect every agent to one shared bus that carries all messages, and let each member decide which messages to act on.
patterns.figure_caption: Every message reaches every member, and each member does its own filtering.

patterns.title: Polling Pub/Sub
patterns.gist: Publishers add events to a shared store, and each subscriber agent checks it on its own schedule using a saved cursor.
patterns.figure_caption: Events wait in the store. The subscriber pulls whatever is newer than its cursor.

patterns.title: Microservices Messaging
patterns.gist: Agent services talk through message channels, so a sender posts work and moves on without waiting for the receiver.
patterns.figure_caption: The sender only needs the channel to be up. Acknowledgements and the dead-letter queue stop messages from vanishing.

patterns.title: Microservices Aggregator
patterns.gist: One aggregator calls several specialist subagents, then merges their partial outputs into a single answer for the user.
patterns.figure_caption: The user asks once and gets one answer. The aggregator hides the specialists and names any gaps.

patterns.title: Saga
patterns.gist: Run a multi-step job across agents as a chain of steps, each paired with an action that undoes it.
patterns.figure_caption: Forward steps commit one by one. A failure runs the recorded compensations backwards.

patterns.title: Commander
patterns.gist: A commander agent pushes a multi-service job through to the end, retrying failed steps from a saved log until all succeed.
patterns.figure_caption: The commander keeps retrying and logging until every step is done, without rolling back.

patterns.title: Distributed Tracing
patterns.gist: Carry one trace id through the orchestrator, subagents, tool calls and model calls, so a whole run reads as one tree.
patterns.figure_caption: The same trace id rides along every hop, so every span lands in one tree.

patterns.title: Log Aggregation
patterns.gist: Send logs from every agent run, subagent and MCP server to one central store, indexed by run id, for search and alerts.
patterns.figure_caption: Scattered logs on each machine become one searchable record keyed by run id.

patterns.title: Self-Registration
patterns.gist: Each agent service or MCP server tells a registry its name, address and tools at startup, and keeps renewing that entry.
patterns.figure_caption: The service announces itself and keeps its entry alive. Silence gets it removed.

patterns.title: Service Locator
patterns.gist: Code asks a central locator for a connector or agent by name while running, instead of having each one handed in.
patterns.figure_caption: Callers know only a name. The locator decides which live connector answers to it.

patterns.title: Promise
patterns.gist: Give back a placeholder for a result that will arrive later, so the caller keeps working instead of waiting.
patterns.figure_caption: The caller gets a handle at once and the result later.

patterns.title: Async Method Invocation
patterns.gist: Start a slow job, like a background subagent, get a future (a claim ticket for the result) at once, and collect the result later.
patterns.figure_caption: The invoker returns a task id now and delivers the result later, by polling or by callback.

patterns.title: Event-Based Asynchronous
patterns.gist: Show a long job as events (start, progress, completed, failed, cancel), so the UI and agent loop react as things happen.
patterns.figure_caption: One running job raises separate events that different subscribers act on.

patterns.title: Producer-Consumer
patterns.gist: Many sources put agent jobs into a bounded (size-limited) buffer, and a separate set of workers takes them off at its own pace.
patterns.figure_caption: Producers and consumers never meet, and the bounded buffer sets the pace for both.

patterns.title: Event Queue
patterns.gist: Hold events that arrive mid-turn in a queue, so the agent loop handles them in order at a safe point.
patterns.figure_caption: Events wait in the inbox until the loop reaches a turn boundary.

patterns.title: Active Object
patterns.gist: Give a scheduled task its own thread and request queue, so callers add requests and get futures back.
patterns.figure_caption: Callers only add requests, and the task's own thread does all the work.

patterns.title: Reactor
patterns.gist: Run one event loop that waits on many streaming connections at once and sends each ready event to its handler.
patterns.figure_caption: One wait covers every connection, and ready ones go to their handlers.

patterns.title: Thread-Pool Executor
patterns.gist: Run tool calls or whole sessions on a fixed set of reusable workers, so extra load waits in a queue instead of creating endless threads.
patterns.figure_caption: Work waits in a queue for a fixed set of reused workers instead of creating more threads.

patterns.title: Thread-Specific Storage
patterns.gist: Give each session its own slot for user id, budget and trace id, which shared code can read without passing it everywhere.
patterns.figure_caption: The same shared code reads a different slot, depending on which task runs it.

patterns.title: Guarded Suspension
patterns.gist: Pause an action until its condition is true, such as waiting for the user's approval before running a risky tool.
patterns.figure_caption: The tool call sleeps at the gate until the guard turns true.

patterns.title: Balking
patterns.gist: If an object is not in the right state, return at once instead of waiting, such as skipping a run already in progress.
patterns.figure_caption: A request that arrives mid-run is refused on the spot, not queued.

patterns.title: Poison Pill
patterns.gist: Shut down queue workers cleanly by sending a special stop message that each worker recognises and exits on.
patterns.figure_caption: The stop signal travels through the queue behind the real work.

patterns.title: Half-Sync/Half-Async
patterns.gist: Let clients use simple blocking calls while the backend runs model streams and tool calls asynchronously, joined by a queue.
patterns.figure_caption: Blocking code above, non-blocking code below, and a queue in between.

patterns.title: Monitor
patterns.gist: Wrap shared session state in an object whose methods run one at a time, with wait and notify for conditions.
patterns.figure_caption: One caller is inside at a time, and waiters park in the wait set until notified.

patterns.title: Lockable Object
patterns.gist: Let a caller lock a session object across a change of several steps, so other writers wait or back off until it is released.
patterns.figure_caption: The holder keeps the lock across several steps while others are turned away.

patterns.title: Double-Checked Locking
patterns.gist: Create a shared client only when first needed, checking once without the lock and again under it, so only one thread builds it.
patterns.figure_caption: The second check, made under the lock, stops a racing thread from building twice.

patterns.title: Double Buffer
patterns.gist: Keep two buffers: the UI shows the finished one while the stream fills the other, then they swap in one step.
patterns.figure_caption: Writers fill the back buffer, readers see only the front, and a swap exchanges them.

patterns.title: Intercepting Filter
patterns.gist: Pass every prompt and response through a chain of guardrail filters, each able to inspect, rewrite or block it.
patterns.figure_caption: Traffic in both directions passes a chain of separate filters, and any of them can stop it.

patterns.title: Specification
patterns.gist: Write permission rules as small predicates (yes-or-no tests) combined with and, or and not, then test each action against them.
patterns.figure_caption: Small reusable rules combine into a tree that judges each proposed action.

patterns.title: Filterer
patterns.gist: Give a tool or content collection a filtered() method that returns a smaller collection of the same type, chained per session.
patterns.figure_caption: Each filtered() call returns the same type, so the narrowing can go on.

patterns.title: Role Object
patterns.gist: Attach role objects such as editor or operator to a session while it runs, each carrying the permissions it grants.
patterns.figure_caption: The session stays the same object while roles come and go around it.

patterns.title: Bulkhead
patterns.gist: Split sandboxes, worker pools and quotas per session or tenant (customer), so one runaway agent cannot sink the others.
patterns.figure_caption: A flooded compartment stays flooded alone, and its neighbours keep serving.

patterns.title: Idempotent Consumer
patterns.gist: Record each trigger firing's key before acting, so a message delivered twice is recognised and the email is never sent twice.
patterns.figure_caption: A redelivery that finds its key done stops, and one that finds it pending retries with the same key.

patterns.title: Transactional Outbox
patterns.gist: Write the planned side effect to an outbox in the same transaction as the transcript turn, then let a relay carry it out.
patterns.figure_caption: The decision and the pending action commit together, and the relay acts afterwards.

patterns.title: Health Check
patterns.gist: Probe connectors, browsers and remote devices on a schedule, and send work only to the ones that report healthy.
patterns.figure_caption: Regular probes keep a status board that the router trusts before each call.

patterns.title: Immutable
patterns.gist: Make transcript entries, configs and policies read-only once created, so any change makes a new version and history stays intact.
patterns.figure_caption: History can only grow, so an edit attempt is refused and a new entry is added instead.

patterns.title: Private Class Data
patterns.gist: Seal credentials in an inner object that tool code can use through one method but never read, print or pass to the model.
patterns.figure_caption: Each outer ring can use the secret only through the narrow door of the ring inside it.

patterns.title: RAIIResource Acquisition Is Initialization
patterns.gist: Tie a sandbox, browser or temp workspace to a scope, so it is released on every exit path, including errors and cancellation.
patterns.figure_caption: Every way out of the scope passes through the same release step.

patterns.title: Notification
patterns.gist: Collect every guardrail and validation error in one notification object, then report them together instead of failing on the first.
patterns.figure_caption: Every validator writes to one shared report, which goes back in a single reply.

patterns.title: Hexagonal Architecture
patterns.gist: Put the agent core in the middle, and let every model, tool, store and screen plug in through a named port.
patterns.figure_caption: The core talks only to ports, so adapters on either side can be swapped without touching it.

patterns.title: Onion Architecture
patterns.gist: Put the agent's core logic at the centre, and make every outer layer depend inward, never outward.
patterns.figure_caption: Dependencies point inward, and the parts that change often live on the outside.

patterns.title: Clean Architecture
patterns.gist: Arrange the harness in four rings (entities, use cases, adapters, frameworks), with every code dependency pointing inward.
patterns.figure_caption: Use cases own the ports. Controllers carry data in and presenters carry it out.

patterns.title: Layered Architecture
patterns.gist: Stack the harness as UI, API, agent runtime and providers, where each layer calls only the layer just below it.
patterns.figure_caption: Each layer calls only the one below, so the UI can never reach a provider directly.

patterns.title: Monolithic Architecture
patterns.gist: Run the UI server, agent loop, tool runner, scheduler and storage in one process, shipped and scaled as one unit.
patterns.figure_caption: Everything shares one process. The only network trip is the call to the model.

patterns.title: Event-Driven Architecture
patterns.gist: Every harness part publishes typed events and reacts to them, so the loop never calls the UI, store or meter directly.
patterns.figure_caption: Senders publish once. Each listener picks the events it needs.

patterns.title: CQRSCommand Query Responsibility Segregation
patterns.gist: Send user requests down a command path, and show the transcript from a separate read model fed by events.
patterns.figure_caption: Commands change state on one side. The transcript is read from a separate view on the other.

patterns.title: Anti-Corruption Layer
patterns.gist: Translate every MCP server's odd schemas, names and error shapes into one standard tool model before core code sees them.
patterns.figure_caption: Three formats go in, and one standard tool model comes out.

patterns.title: Strangler
patterns.gist: Move traffic one intent at a time from an old prompt chain to a new agent loop, until you can delete the old chain.
patterns.figure_caption: A router moves traffic to the new loop one intent at a time, guided by evals.

patterns.title: Backends For Frontends
patterns.gist: Give each surface (CLI, web, team chat) its own thin backend that fits one shared agent core to that surface.
patterns.figure_caption: Each surface gets a backend shaped for it, and all of them share one core.

patterns.title: API Gateway
patterns.gist: Put one entry point in front of all harness services. It checks identity, limits request rates and routes each request.
patterns.figure_caption: One door checks every request once, then routes it by path.

patterns.title: Feature Toggle
patterns.gist: Decide for each account and session which tools, skills and artifact types exist, by reading flags when the session is built.
patterns.figure_caption: Flags are read once at session start and decide what the model can see.

patterns.title: Component
patterns.gist: Build an agent as a thin entity that carries plug-in components (skills, MCP servers, memory, hooks), each adding tools and prompt text.
patterns.figure_caption: The entity is just a carrier. Behaviour comes from the components bolted onto it.

patterns.title: Subclass Sandbox
patterns.gist: Let plugin and skill authors subclass one base class, and build behaviour only from the safe building blocks it provides.
patterns.figure_caption: Subclasses only touch the base class, and every building block passes through the sandbox.

patterns.title: Dependency Injection
patterns.gist: Build the model client, tool registry and stores at startup, and pass them into an agent loop that never builds its own.
patterns.figure_caption: The loop gets its helpers ready-made and never builds them itself.

patterns.title: Service Layer
patterns.gist: Offer the harness through a few app operations, such as create_session and send_turn, that every surface calls the same way.
patterns.figure_caption: Every surface calls the same few operations, which direct everything behind them.

patterns.title: Business Delegate
patterns.gist: Give app code a local client that hides how the remote harness is found, called and retried, and how it fails.
patterns.figure_caption: App code makes one local call. The delegate handles lookup, retries and error shapes.

patterns.title: Session Facade
patterns.gist: Offer one big remote call that does a whole job on the server, so clients do not chain many small calls.
patterns.figure_caption: One remote call goes in, many local calls run behind the facade, and one handle comes out.

patterns.title: Separated Interface
patterns.gist: Keep SDK interfaces in one package and their implementations in others, so code depends on the contract, never a provider.
patterns.figure_caption: The core and implementations both point at the interface package, never at each other.

patterns.title: Domain Model
patterns.gist: Put turn-handling rules inside rich objects like Conversation, Turn and ToolCall, so behaviour lives with the data it protects.
patterns.figure_caption: The handler calls one method. The objects enforce the rules among themselves.

patterns.title: Transaction Script
patterns.gist: Handle each request with one procedure that runs top to bottom: load rows, call the model, run tools, write rows, return.
patterns.figure_caption: Each request has its own straight-line procedure that talks to the database directly.

patterns.title: Table Module
patterns.gist: Write one module per table or collection (sessions, messages, tool_calls) that holds the logic for all its rows at once.
patterns.figure_caption: One module per table works on whole record sets, which pass from module to module.

patterns.title: Collection Pipeline
patterns.gist: Prepare the transcript for the model as a chain of filter, map and take steps over the message list.
patterns.figure_caption: Each operation returns a new list, smaller or cleaner than the last.

patterns.title: Function Composition
patterns.gist: Build one tool-result formatter by joining small single-purpose functions, then reuse that joined function everywhere.
patterns.figure_caption: Small functions snap together into one function that is applied once.

patterns.title: Combinator
patterns.gist: Build complex permission rules or output checkers from a few basic checks and operators such as all_of, any_of and not_.
patterns.figure_caption: Operators combine checks into a bigger check of the same shape.

patterns.title: Currying
patterns.gist: Turn a tool runner with many inputs into a chain of one-input functions, fixing the sandbox at startup and permissions per session.
patterns.figure_caption: Each stage fixes one argument and hands on a smaller function.

patterns.title: Monad
patterns.gist: Chain tool steps that return Result values (a success or an error), so the first error skips the rest and arrives as one clean failure.
patterns.figure_caption: Steps run on the Ok track, and the first Err skips straight to the end.

patterns.title: MVCModel-View-Controller
patterns.gist: Split the chat app into three parts: a model that holds the conversation, a view that shows it, and a controller that changes it.
patterns.figure_caption: Input goes through the controller. The view reads the model, never the controller.

patterns.title: MVPModel-View-Presenter
patterns.gist: Make the transcript view passive. A presenter reads the conversation, decides what to show, and tells the view what to display.
patterns.figure_caption: The view and the model never touch. The presenter sits between them.

patterns.title: Model-View-ViewModel
patterns.gist: Bind chat widgets to a view model's watched fields, so typing, streaming and busy states stay in sync without hand-written glue code.
patterns.figure_caption: Bindings keep widgets and view model fields in sync, with no hand-written glue.

patterns.title: MVIModel-View-Intent
patterns.gist: Turn every click and stream event into an intent, fold it into one fixed state, and draw the whole chat from that state.
patterns.figure_caption: One loop: intent in, new state out, and the view redrawn from the state alone.

patterns.title: Flux
patterns.gist: Send every action through one dispatcher to several stores, each updating its own part, so chat views refresh in one direction.
patterns.figure_caption: One dispatcher sends each action to all stores. Every store updates only its own part.

patterns.title: Bloc
patterns.gist: Feed screen events into a component's input and listen to the stream of states it sends back, so one Send gives many states.
patterns.figure_caption: One event goes in, and a stream of states comes out over time.

patterns.title: Presentation Model
patterns.gist: Keep the chat screen's state and behaviour in a plain object that several thin views copy from and tests use directly.
patterns.figure_caption: One screen model class, usable on any screen, feeds several thin views and is tested on its own.

patterns.title: Front Controller
patterns.gist: Send every request to the harness server through one entry handler that checks identity, logs, and passes it to the right handler.
patterns.figure_caption: Every request passes the same checks before any handler sees it.

patterns.title: Page Controller
patterns.gist: Give each screen of the harness app, such as sessions, chat and settings, its own controller that handles its route.
patterns.figure_caption: Each route has its own controller and view. The router only links paths to controllers.

patterns.title: Composite View
patterns.gist: Build the transcript as a tree of message parts, so text, tool cards and artifact cards all draw through one shared interface.
patterns.figure_caption: Messages and blocks share one interface, so a new piece of text finds its leaf by walking the tree.

patterns.title: Template View
patterns.gist: Draw tool cards and status lines from page templates with blanks, filled from the content block's fields when shown.
patterns.figure_caption: The layout lives in the template. Each block only supplies values for its gaps.

patterns.title: View Helper
patterns.gist: Move markdown display, code colouring and number formatting out of views into small helpers that every view calls.
patterns.figure_caption: Views keep only layout. Every formatting rule lives once, in a shared helper.

patterns.title: Service to Worker
patterns.gist: Run the turn to the end first, then choose and draw a result view, so views only show results that already exist.
patterns.figure_caption: The work finishes before any view is chosen or drawn.

patterns.title: Client-Side UI Composition
patterns.gist: Let the chat shell build its screen from pieces owned by separate services: the transcript, the artifact viewer and widgets.
patterns.figure_caption: Each service ships its own piece. The shell only lays them out and passes messages.

patterns.title: Naked Objects
patterns.gist: Build approval cards and input forms straight from each tool's JSON schema, so a new tool gets a working screen with no new screen code.
patterns.figure_caption: The schema the model already uses becomes the form the user approves.

patterns.title: Data Locality
patterns.gist: Put stable content first in the prompt and keep a session's often-used data together, so caches hit and loads stay cheap.
patterns.figure_caption: Stable bytes at the start get reused. Only the changing end is computed fresh.

patterns.title: Spatial Partition
patterns.gist: Split the embedding space into regions, so a memory or code search checks only the few cells nearest the query.
patterns.figure_caption: The query visits two nearby cells and never touches the other sixty-two.

patterns.title: Arrange/Act/Assert
patterns.gist: Build each eval case in three steps: set up a sample conversation and fakes, run the agent, then check the transcript.
patterns.figure_caption: Setup, one run, then checks: each phase stays in its own box.

patterns.title: Object Mother
patterns.gist: Give evals a factory of named, ready-made test setups, such as an angry customer or a session waiting on an approval.
patterns.figure_caption: Evals ask for setups by name. One class knows how to build them correctly.

patterns.title: Page Object
patterns.gist: Hide a chat screen's selectors behind methods like send() and approve_tool(), so evals and browser agents speak in user actions.
patterns.figure_caption: Callers speak in user actions. Only the page object knows the selectors.

patterns.title: Service Stub
patterns.gist: Replace the model and MCP servers with fakes that give scripted answers, so agent tests run fast, free and the same every time.
patterns.figure_caption: The real loop runs against scripted stand-ins for the model and the tools.

patterns.title: Monostate
patterns.gist: Let code create as many config objects as it likes, while every one reads and writes the same shared state.
patterns.figure_caption: Many instances, one dictionary: a change through any one is seen by all.

patterns.title: Mute Idiom
patterns.gist: Catch and ignore one specific, expected, harmless error, such as a failed best-effort cleanup, and explain why in the code.
patterns.figure_caption: One named, harmless error is ignored. Everything else still shows up.

patterns.title: CRTPCuriously Recurring Template Pattern
patterns.gist: Give SDK base classes the concrete subclass as a type parameter, so shared chained methods return the specific builder or client type.
patterns.figure_caption: The base is told its subclass, so shared methods hand back the specific type.

patterns.title: Twin
patterns.gist: Pair sync and async clients as two linked objects over one shared state, instead of one class that inherits from both.
patterns.figure_caption: Two halves, each with its own parent, linked to each other and to one state.
